medical.title: Mouse study reveals molecular link between high-fat diets and impaired brain function
medical.summary: The molecular mechanisms linking a high-calorie diet to cognitive impairment remain unclear. Researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan, investigated this association in mice, finding that the diet reduced expression of the nuclear protein PQBP1, disrupting the alternative splicing of genes involved in synaptic function. This was associated with synaptic abnormalities and cognitive impairment.

medical.title: High-nicotine e-cigarettes linked to rising nicotine dependence among young adults
medical.summary: Researchers from the University of California San Diego Herbert Wertheim School of Public Health and Human Longevity Science have found that high-nicotine e-cigarette use rose sharply among young adults between 2017 and 2022 and was associated with increased nicotine dependence and more persistent vaping.

medical.title: Substantially more people likely vaping, and more frequently, in US since 2013–14
medical.summary: More people have likely been vaping, and with greater frequency, in the U.S. since 2013–14, suggests a data analysis published online in the journal Tobacco Control.

medical.title: Americans are putting more additives—and calories—in their coffee
medical.summary: While Americans have been drinking roughly the same amount of coffee over recent years, the calories in those cups have increased thanks primarily to the addition of nondairy creamer, according to a new study from researchers at the Gerald J. and Dorothy R. Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy at Tufts University.

medical.title: Motor neurons activate unexpected defense to clear ALS-linked protein before it clumps
medical.summary: ALS is a disease in which, in most cases, a protein forms aggregates in neurons, leading to the rapid loss of motor control and death. A Nagoya University research team has discovered in human neuron cell cultures and mice an unexpected defense mechanism that neurons switch on to avoid these aggregates, offering a new potential path to developing a treatment.

medical.title: Cranberry juice may be a boon for oral hygiene
medical.summary: Boil them, mash them, simmer them in a sauce. Whether they're sweetening a salad, garnishing a cocktail or brightening up home decor, cranberries are an iconic ingredient in holiday festivities. UIC College of Dentistry researcher Christine Wu found another reason to add these tart treats to your grocery cart: oral health.

medical.title: Stigmatizing patient details can push AI to deprioritize high-risk emergency cases
medical.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven tools used in emergency triage may be susceptible to the same clinical stigmas associated with human assessments, researchers at UT Southwestern Medical Center reported in a study published in npj Digital Medicine. Their findings suggest this could result in harmful biases and wrongful prioritization of patients.

medical.title: New biological model proposes why postpartum vulvar pain persists after hormones recover
medical.summary: A new biological model published in Sexual Medicine Reviews by Oxford University Press addresses why pain during sex after childbirth—reported by 60% of women at three months—persists for some long after hormones return to normal. Developed by Dr. Laura Kelly of the Ronin Institute for Independent Scholarship 2.0, the Postpartum Vulvar Tissue-State Model maps five biological systems that change after delivery and recover on distinct timelines.

medical.title: Targeting lung cancer's cellular shipping system could offer a new way to slow tumor growth
medical.summary: A UTHealth Houston-led team has identified a promising new avenue to curb the growth and spread of tumors associated with hard-to-treat lung and other cancers.

medical.title: South Africa's HPV vaccination drive to protect girls from cervical cancer is working—what we know after 10 years
medical.summary: South Africa introduced a vaccination for human papillomavirus (HPV) in public schools in 2014. The program offered the vaccination to fourth-grade girls ages 9 and older. Uptake was high from the start. About 87% of eligible girls received at least one dose during the first year.

medical.title: Millions of children aren't getting vaccinated: How mapping tools can help find them
medical.summary: Worldwide about 13.5 million children have never received a vaccine at all. These are known as zero-dose children. Reaching them is central to the Immunization Agenda 2030, a global drive to ensure that everyone has access to the vaccines they need. Gavi, the vaccine alliance, has built its strategy around finding and reaching them.

medical.title: Older breast cancer survivors fall through Medicare home health gap
medical.summary: Among the increasing number of women who survive breast cancer, many older, long-term survivors remain frail. A new study out today in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute shows that in a given year, over half of these highly frail survivors had no Medicare home health care.

medical.title: Immune mechanism discovery could help predict which early breast cancers will spread
medical.summary: Immune cells that normally protect the body from infection can also drive the progression of some early breast cancers, McGill University researchers have found.

medical.title: Low vitamin D use in patients on enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs raises concerns
medical.summary: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (ASDs) are associated with increased odds of incident osteoporosis or osteopenia, but vitamin D supplementation is underutilized, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American Neurological Association, held from Oct. 17 to 20 in San Diego.

medical.title: Fridge‑free vaccines could reach more people, but there are still practical challenges in African settings
medical.summary: Keeping vaccines and medicines at the right temperature is critical for their efficacy and safety. But this is an often overlooked part of getting them to the people who need them. In April 2025, the U.K. biotechnology company Stablepharma began the first human trial of a tetanus-diphtheria vaccine designed to remain stable without refrigeration. The development has renewed interest in technologies that could do the job, particularly in places where electricity, transport and storage infrastructure are limited. We spoke to immunization experts Charles Shey Wiysonge and Chinwe Juliana Iwu-Jaja about this.

medical.title: Q&A: Gene editing is coming for common diseases. Cardiologists discuss if we are ready
medical.summary: Gene therapy is no longer the future of medicine—it's reality. Treatments that replace, silence or edit genes are already changing clinical care.

medical.title: New microscopy technology may help detect neurological diseases before neurons die
medical.summary: Scientists studying amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and other neurological diseases are getting unprecedented views inside brain cells, using powerful new microscopes to uncover changes that may begin long before neurons die. These technologies enable researchers to zoom in on individual neurons and the tiny structures inside them, watch cells at work in real time and use artificial intelligence to identify patterns linked to disease, according to experts who spoke at the Oct. 18 Presidential Symposium—"Advances in Microscopy for Visualizing Neurologic Disease"—at the 151st Annual Meeting of the American Neurological Association (ANA 2026).

medical.title: Nutritional supplement may help ease 'brain fog' after breast cancer treatment
medical.summary: A new study led by researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center found that a nutritional supplement containing oxaloacetate, a molecule naturally found in the body that helps cells produce energy, may help improve cognitive function and reduce the fatigue experienced by some breast cancer survivors following treatment.

medical.title: Q&A: AI tool automates echocardiogram assessment of the heart's right ventricle
medical.summary: A new study develops and tests DROID-RV, a deep learning model that estimates right ventricular size and function from echocardiograms, and assesses how those estimates relate to later health outcomes. Mostafa Al-Alusi, M.D., M.S., and Patrick T. Ellinor, M.D., Ph.D., of the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute, are the lead and senior authors of a paper published in Nature Cardiovascular Research, "Deep Learning-Enabled Assessment of Right Ventricular Size and Function is Associated with Cardiovascular Outcomes."

medical.title: Prenatal supplement linked to improved child cognition and social behavior
medical.summary: A nutritional supplement taken during pregnancy may support fetal brain development and improve children's cognitive performance and social behavior, according to new research from the University of Colorado Anschutz.

medical.title: Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
medical.summary: Depression may not be one biological condition, but several distinct patterns of brain activity hiding under the same diagnosis. Researchers studying 263 people with depression identified five brain profiles, each showing different patterns of communication between brain regions and associations with symptoms such as anxiety, trauma, and substance abuse.

science.title: Male seahorse pouch proteins may help remove toxic waste from developing embryos
science.summary: Male seahorses, fishes that belong to the Syngnathidae family, show a distinctive reproductive strategy in which males carry developing embryos in a brood pouch. Their most distinctive feature is the brood pouch on the ventral side of the male fish, into which the female fish transfers her eggs.

science.title: Diverse and sustained social activities may boost cognition in older age
science.summary: Diverse and sustained social activities may boost cognitive performance and slow the decline in brain health associated with aging, suggest the findings of a large international study, published online in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health.

science.title: Soybean waste yields 3D-printable material that could help repair skin
science.summary: Transforming a soybean processing byproduct into a material for skin protection and repair is the prospect outlined by a study that used okara, a residue from the production of tofu and soy-based beverages, to obtain a bioactive, biodegradable, 3D-printable biomaterial.

science.title: Are transgender sports bans really about protecting women? Survey data tells a different story
science.summary: Relatively few transgender athletes participate in high school and collegiate sports. Still, since 2020, 27 states have passed laws banning them from participating in sports based on their gender identity.

science.title: A hidden rivalry between two quantum states at the heart of superconductors
science.summary: Transmitting electricity without losing any energy may sound impossible, yet this is precisely the promise of superconductivity. For nearly 40 years, scientists have been working to understand materials that exhibit this remarkable property at relatively high temperatures. Unlocking their secrets could one day help make power grids more efficient, enhance medical technologies and support the development of quantum computing.

science.title: How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics
science.summary: With the U.S. midterms approaching, about one in five voters has asked AI chatbots about elections and politics, a recent survey found.

science.title: New study reveals the high financial value of privacy in legal proceedings
science.summary: A new Management Science study provides rare real-world evidence that people are willing to give up thousands of dollars to prevent sensitive information about their health and income from becoming public. The research, developed over five years by an international team, has now also laid the foundation for a European research project led by Ehud Guttel of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

science.title: Oxygen collisions show evidence of jet quenching, a signature of early-universe matter
science.summary: New results from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) provide strong evidence that smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light generates a quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a type of matter that existed just after the birth of the universe. The data, just published in Physical Review Letters, show that energetic jets of particles lose energy as they traverse the hot, dense matter left in the collision's wake.

science.title: Tofu is the winner. Scientist creates new holistic scoring system to measure the impact of food
science.summary: Consumers are increasingly confronted with conflicting information surrounding how much protein they should have and which protein sources are healthiest, most sustainable, and best value for money. Cambridge research has uncovered the truth.

science.title: Using eyedrops in space—wearable patch offers a new approach
science.summary: Applying eyedrops is difficult in space, where there is almost no gravity. A KAIST research team has developed a wearable patch that delivers eyedrops to the eye without relying on gravity. The research team was led by Professor Ki-Hun Jeong from the Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, in collaboration with a research team led by Professor Se Joon Woo from Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. The paper is published in the journal Sensors and Actuators B: Chemical.

science.title: Why is it so hard to spot a liar? Expert explains the psychology of deception
science.summary: From The Traitors to everyday life, we often mistake nervousness, confidence or group suspicion for signs of deception. Dr Nadja Heym, Associate Professor in Personality Psychology and Psychopathology, explains why spotting a liar is harder than we think.

science.title: Distrust in the media and courts can cause democratic backsliding, study suggests
science.summary: Democratic backsliding can be tricky to spot.

science.title: Supercomputer reveals how size could shape the future of nanomedicine
science.summary: Scientists have long been interested in cellular nanodiscs, tiny particles made from natural cell membranes that mimic many of the functions of living cells. While previous studies demonstrated the therapeutic potential of nanodiscs for drug delivery, detoxification and vaccines, one fundamental question remained unanswered: How does size influence how well they work?

science.title: Water as we've never known it: Physicists test water beyond Earth-like conditions
science.summary: Water isn't always as it seems. Under extreme conditions, such as those found on other planets, it has been discovered to change its atomic structure, giving it the means to alter its appearance and other properties.

science.title: Aurora supercomputer powers two of the largest cosmological simulations to date
science.summary: Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory have completed two of the largest cosmological simulations ever performed. Each simulation modeled the evolution of 13.4 trillion dark matter particles across a region 28.6 billion light-years wide.

science.title: 'Smoking gun' may help solve mystery of high-temperature superconductivity
science.summary: Superconductivity has many important practical applications, including creating powerful magnets used in high-resolution medical scans, transporting electricity efficiently and building ultrasensitive measuring devices. Until now, understanding exactly what lay behind this unique phenomenon at high temperatures has eluded scientists over many decades.

science.title: Fluorescent reaction maps reveal how catalyst activity changes with operating conditions
science.summary: Catalysts spur chemical reactions used across industries, from producing fuels and medicines to manufacturing chemicals and treating pollutants. Improving their performance requires understanding where and how reactions happen on their surfaces. However, conventional measurements average the activity of many catalyst particles, concealing local differences that could hold clues to designing more effective materials.

environment.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
environment.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

environment.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
environment.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

environment.title: As sand becomes more valuable, Sierra Leone’s Mahera Coast grows more vulnerable
environment.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — When the tide pulls away from the beach in the agricultural regions in Mahera in Lungi, about 27 kilometers (17 miles) across the sea from the country’s capital, Freetown, the digging commences. Young men shovel sand into cement bags and carry them to a flat open area to pile sand […]

environment.title: New Zealand builds an arsenal of tools to battle a ‘wily’ invasive seaweed
environment.summary: BAY OF ISLANDS, Aotearoa New Zealand — Since an invasive seaweed called caulerpa was discovered in Aotearoa New Zealand in 2021, forming meadows that blanketed parts of the seabed, it’s taken on an almost mythical status among people who spend time in coastal waters. “It’s so wily and so resilient,” Michele Rogalin-Henderson, a doctoral candidate […]

environment.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
environment.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

environment.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
environment.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

environment.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
environment.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

environment.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
environment.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

environment.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
environment.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

environment.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
environment.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.

mix_items.title: Mouse study reveals molecular link between high-fat diets and impaired brain function
mix_items.summary: The molecular mechanisms linking a high-calorie diet to cognitive impairment remain unclear. Researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan, investigated this association in mice, finding that the diet reduced expression of the nuclear protein PQBP1, disrupting the alternative splicing of genes involved in synaptic function. This was associated with synaptic abnormalities and cognitive impairment.

mix_items.title: Male seahorse pouch proteins may help remove toxic waste from developing embryos
mix_items.summary: Male seahorses, fishes that belong to the Syngnathidae family, show a distinctive reproductive strategy in which males carry developing embryos in a brood pouch. Their most distinctive feature is the brood pouch on the ventral side of the male fish, into which the female fish transfers her eggs.

mix_items.title: Diverse and sustained social activities may boost cognition in older age
mix_items.summary: Diverse and sustained social activities may boost cognitive performance and slow the decline in brain health associated with aging, suggest the findings of a large international study, published online in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health.

mix_items.summary: rezultatele PISA arată că 48% dintre elevii de 15 ani nu ating nivelul minim de competență la citire deși rezultatele sunt îngrijorătoare, acestea pot fi ameliorate printr-o intervenție integrată și susținută, care să răspundă nevoilor copilului și, totodată, să contribuie la dezvoltarea unei rețele de suport capabile să îi ofere sprijinul necesar pe termen lung […] Articolul Competențele de lectură ale elevilor români scad și este nevoie să intervenim. United Way România implementează un program dedicat literației pentru elevii din medii defavorizate apare prima dată în United Way Romania .

mix_items.title: High-nicotine e-cigarettes linked to rising nicotine dependence among young adults
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of California San Diego Herbert Wertheim School of Public Health and Human Longevity Science have found that high-nicotine e-cigarette use rose sharply among young adults between 2017 and 2022 and was associated with increased nicotine dependence and more persistent vaping.

mix_items.title: Substantially more people likely vaping, and more frequently, in US since 2013–14
mix_items.summary: More people have likely been vaping, and with greater frequency, in the U.S. since 2013–14, suggests a data analysis published online in the journal Tobacco Control.

mix_items.title: Americans are putting more additives—and calories—in their coffee
mix_items.summary: While Americans have been drinking roughly the same amount of coffee over recent years, the calories in those cups have increased thanks primarily to the addition of nondairy creamer, according to a new study from researchers at the Gerald J. and Dorothy R. Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy at Tufts University.

mix_items.title: Soybean waste yields 3D-printable material that could help repair skin
mix_items.summary: Transforming a soybean processing byproduct into a material for skin protection and repair is the prospect outlined by a study that used okara, a residue from the production of tofu and soy-based beverages, to obtain a bioactive, biodegradable, 3D-printable biomaterial.

mix_items.title: Motor neurons activate unexpected defense to clear ALS-linked protein before it clumps
mix_items.summary: ALS is a disease in which, in most cases, a protein forms aggregates in neurons, leading to the rapid loss of motor control and death. A Nagoya University research team has discovered in human neuron cell cultures and mice an unexpected defense mechanism that neurons switch on to avoid these aggregates, offering a new potential path to developing a treatment.

mix_items.title: Are transgender sports bans really about protecting women? Survey data tells a different story
mix_items.summary: Relatively few transgender athletes participate in high school and collegiate sports. Still, since 2020, 27 states have passed laws banning them from participating in sports based on their gender identity.

mix_items.title: Cranberry juice may be a boon for oral hygiene
mix_items.summary: Boil them, mash them, simmer them in a sauce. Whether they're sweetening a salad, garnishing a cocktail or brightening up home decor, cranberries are an iconic ingredient in holiday festivities. UIC College of Dentistry researcher Christine Wu found another reason to add these tart treats to your grocery cart: oral health.

mix_items.title: Stigmatizing patient details can push AI to deprioritize high-risk emergency cases
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven tools used in emergency triage may be susceptible to the same clinical stigmas associated with human assessments, researchers at UT Southwestern Medical Center reported in a study published in npj Digital Medicine. Their findings suggest this could result in harmful biases and wrongful prioritization of patients.

mix_items.title: New biological model proposes why postpartum vulvar pain persists after hormones recover
mix_items.summary: A new biological model published in Sexual Medicine Reviews by Oxford University Press addresses why pain during sex after childbirth—reported by 60% of women at three months—persists for some long after hormones return to normal. Developed by Dr. Laura Kelly of the Ronin Institute for Independent Scholarship 2.0, the Postpartum Vulvar Tissue-State Model maps five biological systems that change after delivery and recover on distinct timelines.

mix_items.title: A hidden rivalry between two quantum states at the heart of superconductors
mix_items.summary: Transmitting electricity without losing any energy may sound impossible, yet this is precisely the promise of superconductivity. For nearly 40 years, scientists have been working to understand materials that exhibit this remarkable property at relatively high temperatures. Unlocking their secrets could one day help make power grids more efficient, enhance medical technologies and support the development of quantum computing.

mix_items.title: How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics
mix_items.summary: With the U.S. midterms approaching, about one in five voters has asked AI chatbots about elections and politics, a recent survey found.

mix_items.title: Targeting lung cancer's cellular shipping system could offer a new way to slow tumor growth
mix_items.summary: A UTHealth Houston-led team has identified a promising new avenue to curb the growth and spread of tumors associated with hard-to-treat lung and other cancers.

mix_items.title: South Africa's HPV vaccination drive to protect girls from cervical cancer is working—what we know after 10 years
mix_items.summary: South Africa introduced a vaccination for human papillomavirus (HPV) in public schools in 2014. The program offered the vaccination to fourth-grade girls ages 9 and older. Uptake was high from the start. About 87% of eligible girls received at least one dose during the first year.

mix_items.title: Millions of children aren't getting vaccinated: How mapping tools can help find them
mix_items.summary: Worldwide about 13.5 million children have never received a vaccine at all. These are known as zero-dose children. Reaching them is central to the Immunization Agenda 2030, a global drive to ensure that everyone has access to the vaccines they need. Gavi, the vaccine alliance, has built its strategy around finding and reaching them.

mix_items.title: New study reveals the high financial value of privacy in legal proceedings
mix_items.summary: A new Management Science study provides rare real-world evidence that people are willing to give up thousands of dollars to prevent sensitive information about their health and income from becoming public. The research, developed over five years by an international team, has now also laid the foundation for a European research project led by Ehud Guttel of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

mix_items.title: Older breast cancer survivors fall through Medicare home health gap
mix_items.summary: Among the increasing number of women who survive breast cancer, many older, long-term survivors remain frail. A new study out today in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute shows that in a given year, over half of these highly frail survivors had no Medicare home health care.

mix_items.title: Oxygen collisions show evidence of jet quenching, a signature of early-universe matter
mix_items.summary: New results from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) provide strong evidence that smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light generates a quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a type of matter that existed just after the birth of the universe. The data, just published in Physical Review Letters, show that energetic jets of particles lose energy as they traverse the hot, dense matter left in the collision's wake.

mix_items.title: Immune mechanism discovery could help predict which early breast cancers will spread
mix_items.summary: Immune cells that normally protect the body from infection can also drive the progression of some early breast cancers, McGill University researchers have found.

mix_items.title: Tofu is the winner. Scientist creates new holistic scoring system to measure the impact of food
mix_items.summary: Consumers are increasingly confronted with conflicting information surrounding how much protein they should have and which protein sources are healthiest, most sustainable, and best value for money. Cambridge research has uncovered the truth.

mix_items.title: Using eyedrops in space—wearable patch offers a new approach
mix_items.summary: Applying eyedrops is difficult in space, where there is almost no gravity. A KAIST research team has developed a wearable patch that delivers eyedrops to the eye without relying on gravity. The research team was led by Professor Ki-Hun Jeong from the Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, in collaboration with a research team led by Professor Se Joon Woo from Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. The paper is published in the journal Sensors and Actuators B: Chemical.

mix_items.title: Low vitamin D use in patients on enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs raises concerns
mix_items.summary: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (ASDs) are associated with increased odds of incident osteoporosis or osteopenia, but vitamin D supplementation is underutilized, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American Neurological Association, held from Oct. 17 to 20 in San Diego.

mix_items.title: Why is it so hard to spot a liar? Expert explains the psychology of deception
mix_items.summary: From The Traitors to everyday life, we often mistake nervousness, confidence or group suspicion for signs of deception. Dr Nadja Heym, Associate Professor in Personality Psychology and Psychopathology, explains why spotting a liar is harder than we think.

mix_items.title: Fridge‑free vaccines could reach more people, but there are still practical challenges in African settings
mix_items.summary: Keeping vaccines and medicines at the right temperature is critical for their efficacy and safety. But this is an often overlooked part of getting them to the people who need them. In April 2025, the U.K. biotechnology company Stablepharma began the first human trial of a tetanus-diphtheria vaccine designed to remain stable without refrigeration. The development has renewed interest in technologies that could do the job, particularly in places where electricity, transport and storage infrastructure are limited. We spoke to immunization experts Charles Shey Wiysonge and Chinwe Juliana Iwu-Jaja about this.

mix_items.title: Distrust in the media and courts can cause democratic backsliding, study suggests
mix_items.summary: Democratic backsliding can be tricky to spot.

mix_items.title: Q&A: Gene editing is coming for common diseases. Cardiologists discuss if we are ready
mix_items.summary: Gene therapy is no longer the future of medicine—it's reality. Treatments that replace, silence or edit genes are already changing clinical care.

mix_items.title: New microscopy technology may help detect neurological diseases before neurons die
mix_items.summary: Scientists studying amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and other neurological diseases are getting unprecedented views inside brain cells, using powerful new microscopes to uncover changes that may begin long before neurons die. These technologies enable researchers to zoom in on individual neurons and the tiny structures inside them, watch cells at work in real time and use artificial intelligence to identify patterns linked to disease, according to experts who spoke at the Oct. 18 Presidential Symposium—"Advances in Microscopy for Visualizing Neurologic Disease"—at the 151st Annual Meeting of the American Neurological Association (ANA 2026).

mix_items.title: Supercomputer reveals how size could shape the future of nanomedicine
mix_items.summary: Scientists have long been interested in cellular nanodiscs, tiny particles made from natural cell membranes that mimic many of the functions of living cells. While previous studies demonstrated the therapeutic potential of nanodiscs for drug delivery, detoxification and vaccines, one fundamental question remained unanswered: How does size influence how well they work?

mix_items.title: Water as we've never known it: Physicists test water beyond Earth-like conditions
mix_items.summary: Water isn't always as it seems. Under extreme conditions, such as those found on other planets, it has been discovered to change its atomic structure, giving it the means to alter its appearance and other properties.

mix_items.title: Nutritional supplement may help ease 'brain fog' after breast cancer treatment
mix_items.summary: A new study led by researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center found that a nutritional supplement containing oxaloacetate, a molecule naturally found in the body that helps cells produce energy, may help improve cognitive function and reduce the fatigue experienced by some breast cancer survivors following treatment.

mix_items.title: Aurora supercomputer powers two of the largest cosmological simulations to date
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory have completed two of the largest cosmological simulations ever performed. Each simulation modeled the evolution of 13.4 trillion dark matter particles across a region 28.6 billion light-years wide.

mix_items.title: Q&A: AI tool automates echocardiogram assessment of the heart's right ventricle
mix_items.summary: A new study develops and tests DROID-RV, a deep learning model that estimates right ventricular size and function from echocardiograms, and assesses how those estimates relate to later health outcomes. Mostafa Al-Alusi, M.D., M.S., and Patrick T. Ellinor, M.D., Ph.D., of the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute, are the lead and senior authors of a paper published in Nature Cardiovascular Research, "Deep Learning-Enabled Assessment of Right Ventricular Size and Function is Associated with Cardiovascular Outcomes."

mix_items.title: 'Smoking gun' may help solve mystery of high-temperature superconductivity
mix_items.summary: Superconductivity has many important practical applications, including creating powerful magnets used in high-resolution medical scans, transporting electricity efficiently and building ultrasensitive measuring devices. Until now, understanding exactly what lay behind this unique phenomenon at high temperatures has eluded scientists over many decades.

mix_items.title: Fluorescent reaction maps reveal how catalyst activity changes with operating conditions
mix_items.summary: Catalysts spur chemical reactions used across industries, from producing fuels and medicines to manufacturing chemicals and treating pollutants. Improving their performance requires understanding where and how reactions happen on their surfaces. However, conventional measurements average the activity of many catalyst particles, concealing local differences that could hold clues to designing more effective materials.

mix_items.title: Prenatal supplement linked to improved child cognition and social behavior
mix_items.summary: A nutritional supplement taken during pregnancy may support fetal brain development and improve children's cognitive performance and social behavior, according to new research from the University of Colorado Anschutz.

mix_items.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
mix_items.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

mix_items.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
mix_items.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

mix_items.title: As sand becomes more valuable, Sierra Leone’s Mahera Coast grows more vulnerable
mix_items.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — When the tide pulls away from the beach in the agricultural regions in Mahera in Lungi, about 27 kilometers (17 miles) across the sea from the country’s capital, Freetown, the digging commences. Young men shovel sand into cement bags and carry them to a flat open area to pile sand […]

mix_items.title: New Zealand builds an arsenal of tools to battle a ‘wily’ invasive seaweed

mix_items.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
mix_items.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

mix_items.title: Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
mix_items.summary: Depression may not be one biological condition, but several distinct patterns of brain activity hiding under the same diagnosis. Researchers studying 263 people with depression identified five brain profiles, each showing different patterns of communication between brain regions and associations with symptoms such as anxiety, trauma, and substance abuse.

mix_items.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
mix_items.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

mix_items.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
mix_items.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

mix_items.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
mix_items.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

mix_items.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
mix_items.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

mix_items.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.
